Function / Ileocaecal transit / 1.note: Locate terminal ileum and its mucosa approaching the caecal wall. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Ileocaecal transit / 2.note: The upper and lower lips and their frenula frame the ileal orifice. This is folded bowel tissue in wall context. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Ileocaecal transit / 3.note: Teaching route: terminal ileum → junction → caecal cavity. A visible slit alone does not establish a continuous open lumen. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Ileocaecal transit / 4.note: Reflux competence depends on more than lip appearance; omitted attachment geometry and living muscle behavior cannot be tested in this static opened specimen. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Appendix wall and supply / 1.note: Follow the converging taeniae to the appendix base; this model shows one representative appendix position. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Appendix wall and supply / 2.note: Lymphoid tissue belongs in mucosa and submucosa beneath the exposed luminal surface. It is not a set of free luminal particles. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Appendix wall and supply / 3.note: These enlarged representative follicles provide immune wall context. Cell trafficking, antibody production and microbiota reseeding are not depicted. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Appendix wall and supply / 4.note: Keep mesoappendix visible as the contextual carrier of appendicular supply. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectoanal coordination / 1.note: The rectal ampulla acts as a temporary reservoir. Filling distends the rectal wall; folds remain anatomical landmarks. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectoanal coordination / 2.note: At rest, IAS tone, the EAS complex and puborectalis support continence. The IAS continues from rectal circular smooth muscle. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectoanal coordination / 3.note: Rectal distension triggers the rectoanal inhibitory reflex: IAS relaxation. This reflex alone does not mean defecation occurs. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectoanal coordination / 4.note: When defecation is deferred, voluntary EAS contraction maintains the outlet barrier. The puborectalis sling supports the anorectal bend. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectoanal coordination / 5.note: For evacuation, outlet relaxation is coordinated with propulsive force. Puborectalis relaxation allows the anorectal angle to widen. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectoanal coordination / 6.note: Return to resting continence as outlet muscles resume tone; this state is a qualitative teaching summary, not a timed physiological measurement. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectal arterial routes / 1.note: Arterial inflow: inferior mesenteric artery → superior rectal artery → rectal wall. The proximal origin and terminal microvessels are omitted. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectal arterial routes / 2.note: Middle and inferior rectal arteries contribute to distal territories; they are not present as named vessel meshes. Territories overlap. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectal venous routes / 1.note: The named internal plexus represents only the vascular component of normal anal cushions; normal cushions also contain supporting nonvascular tissue. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectal venous routes / 2.note: Superior route: rectal venous network → superior rectal vein → inferior mesenteric vein → portal circulation. Omitted links are diagram annotations. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectal venous routes / 3.note: Distal venous return also reaches systemic circulation through pelvic veins. Portal–systemic communications are not explicitly reconstructed. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Rectal venous routes / 4.note: Normal cushions, symptomatic hemorrhoidal disease and anorectal varices are different concepts. Purple shape alone depicts none of their clinical diagnoses. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Regional lymphatic routes / 1.note: Mesorectal nodes belong to the mesorectal compartment; they must remain contextualized rather than floating isolated dots. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Regional lymphatic routes / 2.note: A superior route continues through superior rectal lymphatics toward inferior mesenteric nodes, beyond this model. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Regional lymphatic routes / 3.note: Additional rectal drainage reaches internal iliac nodes. Avoid teaching all tissue above the pectinate line as an exclusive mesorectal pathway. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.

Function / Regional lymphatic routes / 4.note: Below the pectinate line, superficial inguinal drainage is the key regional route; these nodes and channels are omitted. Manual teaching state; geometry remains static.
